Designing a Freight Logistics Platform (Uber Freight)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Geo Matching, Real-Time Tracking, Route Optimization, Allocation, WebSocket Asked at: Uber Freight, Rivigo, BlackBuck, Delhivery, Amazon Logistics Prerequisites: Geospatial Indexing, WebSockets, Message Queues, and Caching

1. Understanding the Problem

A freight logistics platform connects shippers (companies with cargo) to carriers (truck owners/drivers). A shipper posts a shipment request with source, destination, weight, and pickup window. The system finds the best available truck considering proximity, route alignment, and capacity, assigns it, and then provides real-time tracking with accurate ETA to the shipper throughout transit. Unlike ride-sharing (seconds-scale matching), freight operates on minutes-to-hours timescales, but the tracking and ETA requirements are equally real-time.

2. Naive First Cut

New components:

  • API Server: One process taking the shipper’s booking, receiving every truck’s GPS ping, and answering tracking queries.
  • Postgres DB: Trucks, shipments and each truck’s last known position in one database.
  • Truck GPS: The device bolted into each truck, reporting where it is every few seconds. It is drawn as a client because it is a traffic source in its own right, and in this design it is by far the heaviest one.

How this breaks:

  • Querying nearest available truck in Postgres with lat/lng requires scanning all trucks with distance calculation – O(N) full table scan💡 O(N) means the work grows in step with the number of trucks, because the only way to find the closest one is to measure the distance to all of them. Doubling the fleet doubles the cost of every booking.
  • Single API server cannot handle 300K+ GPS pings per second from active fleet
  • No way to push live location updates to shippers – polling is wasteful and adds latency
  • If two shippers request similar routes simultaneously and the same truck is best for both – double-assignment
  • ETA is static – computed once at booking, never updated as truck encounters traffic or delays
  • No route-awareness – system might assign a truck 200km away when another truck is on the same highway heading toward the pickup

The rest of the doc evolves this into a production-grade allocation and tracking system.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Uber Freight Marketplace – Real-time load matching platform connecting shippers with carriers. Uses scoring algorithms that weight price, carrier reliability, proximity, and route alignment. (Uber Freight Engineering)
  • Convoy Dead-Head Optimization – Minimizes empty miles by matching trucks to loads near their current route terminus. Uses graph-based route planning to batch multiple shipments on a single truck. (Convoy Engineering)💡 Dead-head miles are miles driven with an empty trailer - the truck is burning fuel and the driver is on the clock, and nobody is paying for the load. Cutting them is the main thing a freight marketplace sells to carriers.
  • Uber H3 Hexagonal Grid – Used for geospatial partitioning of supply and demand. Each hexagon represents a region for allocation scoring and demand prediction. (Uber H3)💡 H3 tiles the world in fixed hexagons, each with a short id. Because every neighbouring hexagon is the same distance away, “the cells around this one” is a cheap lookup rather than a distance calculation - which is how a two-dimensional question becomes a key lookup.
  • Google Maps ETA Engine – Real-time traffic-aware routing using live GPS probe data. Historical patterns + live anomalies predict segment-level travel times. Google published this as part of their DeepMind collaboration on traffic prediction.
  • Rivigo Relay Model – Indian freight company that uses relay points every 300km so drivers can be swapped. System must track truck AND driver separately, recompute ETA at each relay. Shows the importance of event-driven state machines for shipment lifecycle.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Shipper books a truck – specify source, destination, weight, goods type, pickup window. System allocates the best available truck.
  2. Real-time tracking – shipper sees live truck position on a map throughout transit with updated ETA.
  3. Smart allocation – system assigns trucks maximizing utilization (minimize deadhead miles) considering proximity, route alignment, capacity, and carrier rating.

Below the Line

  • Carrier can accept/decline assigned loads
  • Multi-stop routes (truck picks up multiple shipments along corridor)
  • Dynamic pricing based on demand and route popularity
  • Shipment status notifications (picked up, in transit, delayed, delivered)
  • Proof of delivery (photo/signature)
  • Invoice and payment settlement

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

Non-functional requirement (NFR) Target
Location ingestion 50K active trucks x 6 pings/min = 300K writes/sec
Allocation latency Truck assigned within 60 seconds of booking request
Tracking freshness Shipper sees location no older than 15 seconds
Booking consistency Strong – no double-assignment of same truck to two shipments
Availability 99.9% – shipper can always book and track
scroll →

💡 Strong consistency here means one specific thing: the moment a truck is assigned, every other booking in flight must see it as taken. Deep Dive 2 is entirely about earning that one line.

Below the Line

  • Estimated time of arrival (ETA) accuracy within 10 minutes of actual arrival
  • Handle 10K bookings/day
  • Sub-second WebSocket push for live tracking
  • Idempotent booking API (retry-safe)

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Fleet: 50K active trucks at peak, 200K registered💡 Back-of-envelope estimation is the rough arithmetic done before any component is chosen, so each pick answers a number. Learn more →
  • Write QPS (queries per second): 300K location pings/sec (GPS devices)💡 Note the shape of this design before reading further: the write rate is three million times the booking rate. The expensive tier and the valuable tier are not the same tier.
  • Booking QPS: ~0.1/sec (10K/day – not the bottleneck)
  • Read QPS: 5K tracking queries/sec (shippers checking shipments)
  • Storage: Tracking history ~473TB/year (50K trucks x 6 pings/sec x 86400 x 365 days x 50 bytes), which is why the trail goes to Cassandra with a retention policy rather than Postgres

7. Core Entities

  • Shipper – company that needs goods moved. Has account, payment method, shipment history.
  • Carrier – trucking company that owns trucks. Has fleet, rating, compliance docs.
  • Truck – physical vehicle. Has capacity, type, current location, status, assigned carrier.
  • Shipment – booking unit. Source, destination, weight, status (state machine), assigned truck.
  • Route – predefined corridor between regions with waypoints, distance, typical duration.
  • LocationPing – ephemeral GPS data. truckId, lat/lng, speed, heading, timestamp.

8. API / System Interface

POST /api/v1/shipments
  Body: { shipperId, pickupLat, pickupLng, dropLat, dropLng, weightTons, goodsType, pickupWindowStart, pickupWindowEnd }
  Response: { shipmentId, assignedTruckId, estimatedPickupTime, eta, status: "ASSIGNED" }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (shipper)
  Note: Idempotent via X-Idempotency-Key header. Never trust client for shipperId -- derive from token.

GET /api/v1/shipments/{shipmentId}/track
  Response: { truckLat, truckLng, speed, heading, eta, lastUpdated, status }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (shipper -- must own this shipment)

WebSocket /ws/v1/shipments/{shipmentId}/live
  Pushes: { truckLat, truckLng, speed, eta, updatedAt } every 10s
  Auth: JWT ticket in connection params

POST /api/v1/trucks/{truckId}/location (called by GPS device)
  Body: { lat, lng, speed, heading, timestamp }
  Response: 204 No Content
  Auth: Device API key
  Note: Fire-and-forget. High volume -- 6 calls/min per truck.

GET /api/v1/shipments/{shipmentId}
  Response: { full shipment details, truck info, timeline of events }
  Auth: JWT Bearer (shipper)

9. High-Level Design

FR1: Shipper Books a Truck

The shipper submits a booking and we find a truck for it. Two services and one database.

Components introduced:

  • Booking Service – validates the request, creates the shipment record, triggers allocation
  • Allocation Service – finds nearby available trucks, ranks them, assigns the best one
  • Postgres – shipments and trucks, including each truck’s last known lat/lng

Flow (numbered steps):

  1. Shipper calls POST /shipments with pickup and drop locations and the weight
  2. API Gateway authenticates and rate-limits, forwards to Booking Service💡 The gateway verifies the shipper’s signed token (a JSON Web Token, or JWT) and reads the shipper’s identity out of it. That is why the API notes say never to take shipperId from the request body - the token is the only trustworthy source.
  3. Booking Service validates inputs and inserts the shipment with status=PENDING
  4. Booking Service calls Allocation Service with the shipment details
  5. Allocation Service finds candidates with a bounding box on the trucks table: WHERE status='AVAILABLE' AND lat BETWEEN ? AND ? AND lng BETWEEN ? AND ?, then filters by capacity and truck type
  6. It ranks the survivors: score = 0.5 * (1/distance) + 0.3 * route_alignment + 0.2 * carrier_rating
  7. It reads the top candidate’s row to confirm the truck is still AVAILABLE
  8. It then writes the assignment: UPDATE trucks SET status='ASSIGNED', current_shipment_id=?
  9. It sets the shipment to ASSIGNED and returns a confirmation

Why rank rather than take the nearest? A truck 10km away heading in the wrong direction is worse than one 30km away already travelling that route, and a carrier with a poor reliability record is worse than both. Distance is one input, not the answer.

What we have deliberately left broken. A shipper can book and gets a sensible truck. Three things are wrong:

  • Steps 7 and 8 are a check followed by a write, as two separate statements. Two bookings landing at the same moment both read the truck as AVAILABLE, both proceed, and the second overwrites the first — so one truck is promised to two shipments and one shipper finds out at the dock. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • Step 5 is a bounding box on lat and lng. A B-tree orders on one dimension and proximity has two, so an index on lat yields a band wrapping the planet and the longitude filter is a scan within it. That gets worse as the fleet grows.💡 A B-tree is the ordinary database index: a sorted tree, which means it can narrow on exactly one column at a time. Two indexes on two columns are not the same thing as one index that understands two dimensions - that is what a geospatial index is for.
  • The confirmation in step 9 includes an ETA we have not worked out how to compute. That is FR3.

FR2: Real-Time Location Tracking

Trucks emit GPS pings and shippers want to watch their shipment move. Both halves reduce to the trucks table FR1 already has.

New components:

  • Location Ingestion Service – accepts a GPS ping and records the truck’s current position

Flow:

  1. Truck GPS device sends its position every 10 seconds to POST /trucks/{id}/location
  2. Location Ingestion Service updates that truck’s row in place — new lat, lng, speed and last_ping — one row per truck, overwritten
  3. The shipper’s app polls GET /shipments/{id}/location every few seconds while the shipment is in transit
  4. The service reads the assigned truck’s row and returns it
  5. The shipper sees the dot move on the map

Why overwrite rather than append a position history? Because the question this page asks is “where is my truck now”, and one row per truck keeps the table at fleet size instead of growing with ping volume. It also means FR1’s allocation query reads current positions for free, from the same rows.

Why does last_ping matter? This is correctness rather than scale, which is why it is here: a truck whose device loses signal keeps its last position forever and would otherwise stay in FR1’s candidate pool as a ghost. Treat anything older than a couple of minutes as stale and exclude it from allocation.

What we have deliberately left broken. Positions are current and shippers can watch them. Two problems, on opposite sides of the system:

  • Step 2 is an indexed UPDATE per ping, at 300K pings/sec. Each one makes Postgres write a new row version, update the lat and lng indexes, append to the write-ahead log (WAL) and leave a dead tuple for vacuum.💡 The WAL is a sequential file Postgres appends every change to before touching the real data, so a crash can be replayed. A “dead tuple” is the superseded old copy of the row, and vacuum is the background job that reclaims it - so one logical overwrite costs several physical writes plus cleanup work later. That is not a tuning problem; it is one to two orders of magnitude past a single primary, and at 300K dead tuples/sec autovacuum falls behind permanently. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Step 3 is polling. Every watching shipper asks every few seconds whether anything changed, and the answer is usually “it moved 40 metres”. It also puts a floor under how fresh the map can be, and that floor is the poll interval. That is Deep Dive 4.

FR3: ETA Computation

FR1’s confirmation promised an ETA. We owe the shipper a number.

New components: none. We know where the truck is and where it is going, so this is arithmetic.

Flow:

  1. At allocation time, compute the straight-line distance from pickup to drop and divide by an assumed average speed
  2. Store the resulting timestamp on the shipment row
  3. The shipper reads it alongside the rest of the shipment

Why compute it at booking? Because that is when the shipper needs it — they are deciding whether to accept the booking, and a number at that moment is worth more than a better number later.

What we have deliberately left broken. There is an ETA and it is close to useless.

Straight-line distance ignores that roads are not straight. A route through hills, around a bay, or along a single permitted truck corridor can be 40% longer than the line between its endpoints, and a fixed average speed ignores terrain, load weight, mandatory driver rest and traffic entirely.

Worse, it is computed once and never revised. A truck stuck for three hours still shows its original arrival time, so the one moment the shipper most needs the ETA to change is the moment it is guaranteed to be wrong — and because we never recompute, nothing in the system knows it is wrong. That is Deep Dive 3.

10. Technology Choices

Tier Purpose Stores Access Pattern Primary Alternatives
Location Store (hot) Real-time truck positions lat/lng per active truck Geo-radius queries + point updates Redis Geo PostGIS, Elasticsearch geo_point
Booking DB Shipments, trucks, assignments Relational data with joins CRUD by shipmentId, truckId Postgres CockroachDB, MySQL
Event Bus Location events and state transitions GPS pings, status changes Pub/sub + ordered per truck Kafka Kinesis, Redpanda
Cache ETA, truck availability, route data Precomputed values High-QPS reads with TTL Redis Memcached
Real-time Delivery Push truck position to shippers WebSocket messages Fan-out per active shipment WebSocket Gateway + Redis Pub/Sub Server-Sent Events (SSE), gRPC streaming
History Store Historical truck paths Time-series GPS data Batch writes, range queries by time Cassandra or TimescaleDB InfluxDB, ClickHouse
Maps/Routing ETA and route computation Road network + traffic Request-response per computation External Maps API (Google/Mapbox) Self-hosted OSRM
scroll →

💡 Cassandra and TimescaleDB are both built for data that only ever gets appended and is read back by time range - which is exactly what a truck’s path is. OSRM is an open-source routing engine you can host yourself if you would rather not pay per Maps API call.

Why Redis Geo over Postgres + PostGIS for truck locations? 300K writes/sec is pure in-memory territory. PostGIS would require disk I/O on every update. Redis Geo uses an in-memory sorted set with geohash encoding – sub-millisecond for both writes and proximity queries.💡 Redis Geo stores coordinates in memory and answers “who is within X km of this point” directly. A geohash turns a latitude and longitude into one short string where nearby places share a prefix, which is the trick that lets a sorted structure answer a two-dimensional question. We only need the latest position per truck (not history), so Redis’s memory footprint stays bounded at ~50K entries.

Why Kafka for GPS pings and not direct Redis writes? If the Location Ingestion service crashes between receiving a ping and writing to Redis, the ping is lost forever. Kafka gives us durability and replay. Consumers can rebuild Redis from Kafka on crash recovery. Also decouples ingestion (300K/sec bursty) from processing (variable consumer speed).💡 That last sentence is backpressure: the log absorbs a burst the consumers cannot keep up with, so the consumers fall behind instead of falling over, and catch up when the burst passes.

Why WebSocket over polling for shipper tracking? A shipper tracking an active shipment wants updates every 10 seconds. With polling: 5K shippers x 1 req/10s = 500 req/sec – wasteful since most responses are “same position.” WebSocket: single connection per active tracker, push only when position changes. Saves bandwidth and reduces latency from 10s (polling interval) to ~100ms (push on update).

11. Data Modeling

Redis Geo (Truck Positions – real-time):

Key: "trucks:available:{region}" -> Geo Set
  Member: truckId
  Score: geohash-encoded lat/lng

Key: "truck:meta:{truckId}" -> Hash
  { status, capacity, type, heading, speed, lastPing, currentShipmentId }
  TTL: 60s (auto-expires if truck stops pinging -- marks as offline)

Key: "eta:{shipmentId}" -> String
  Value: "2026-08-19T14:30:00Z"
  TTL: 120s (recomputed every 2 min)

Postgres (Booking DB):

CREATE TABLE trucks (
    truck_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    carrier_id UUID NOT NULL,
    capacity_tons DECIMAL(6,2),
    truck_type VARCHAR(30),  -- FLATBED, REFRIGERATED, CONTAINER, OPEN
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- AVAILABLE, ASSIGNED, IN_TRANSIT, MAINTENANCE
    current_lat DECIMAL(10,7),
    current_lng DECIMAL(10,7),
    last_location_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_trucks_status ON trucks(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_trucks_carrier ON trucks(carrier_id);

CREATE TABLE shipments (
    shipment_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    shipper_id UUID NOT NULL,
    truck_id UUID,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- PENDING, ASSIGNED, PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, DELIVERED, CANCELLED
    pickup_lat DECIMAL(10,7),
    pickup_lng DECIMAL(10,7),
    drop_lat DECIMAL(10,7),
    drop_lng DECIMAL(10,7),
    weight_tons DECIMAL(6,2),
    goods_type VARCHAR(50),
    pickup_window_start TIMESTAMP,
    pickup_window_end TIMESTAMP,
    estimated_delivery_at TIMESTAMP,
    actual_delivery_at TIMESTAMP,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
    assigned_at TIMESTAMP,
    idempotency_key UUID UNIQUE
);
CREATE INDEX idx_shipments_shipper ON shipments(shipper_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_shipments_truck ON shipments(truck_id, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_shipments_status ON shipments(status);

CREATE TABLE routes (
    route_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    source_region VARCHAR(50),
    dest_region VARCHAR(50),
    waypoints JSONB,  -- [{lat, lng, name}]
    distance_km INT,
    typical_duration_hours DECIMAL(5,2)
);

Kafka Topics:

Topic: truck-location-pings (partitioned by truckId)
  Key: truckId
  Value: { truckId, lat, lng, speed, heading, timestamp }
  Retention: 24 hours

Topic: shipment-events (partitioned by shipmentId)
  Key: shipmentId
  Value: { shipmentId, eventType, truckId, timestamp, metadata }
  Events: CREATED, ASSIGNED, PICKED_UP, IN_TRANSIT, DELAYED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED
  Retention: 7 days

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Find nearest available trucks Redis Geo GEOSEARCH trucks:available:{region} FROMLONLAT lng lat BYRADIUS 100 km COUNT 20 ASC
Update truck position Redis Geo GEOADD trucks:available:{region} lng lat truckId (from Kafka consumer)
Assign truck to shipment Postgres UPDATE trucks SET status='ASSIGNED' WHERE truck_id=? AND status='AVAILABLE' (row lock)

12. Deep Dives

1) 300K pings a second, each an indexed UPDATE. What absorbs that?

Problem: FR2 updates a truck’s row on every ping. The row is indexed on lat and lng because FR1’s allocation query needs it, so the read path and the write path are fighting over the same structure.

Bad: write every GPS ping directly to Postgres, which is what FR2 built. One ping is not one write: Postgres creates a new row version, updates both geo indexes, appends to the write-ahead log, and leaves a dead tuple behind. Call it a handful of disk operations, so 300K pings/sec becomes low millions of write operations a second against one primary.

Three distinct things break, worth separating because they fail on different timescales:

  • Throughput is one to two orders of magnitude past a single primary, immediately.
  • Index churn means the indexes that make FR1’s allocation tolerable are exactly what makes this write expensive — the two requirements are in direct conflict over the same B-trees.
  • Vacuum falls behind permanently at 300K dead tuples/sec, so the table bloats and reads get slower over time even though the row count never grows. That one appears days later and is the hardest to diagnose.

And note what we are paying for: a truck parked at a depot sends the same coordinate hundreds of times, and we do the full write every time to store a value that did not change.

  • At 300K writes/sec, Postgres row-level locking on the trucks table creates massive contention. WAL becomes the bottleneck. Response times degrade to seconds.

2) Two bookings claim the same truck in the same instant. Who finds out at the dock?

Problem: FR1 reads the truck to confirm it is available, then writes the assignment. Between those two statements, anything can happen.

Bad: exactly what FR1 steps 7 and 8 do — check status='AVAILABLE', then update, as two separate queries. Two bookings arriving together both read AVAILABLE, both pass the check, and both write. The second overwrites the first.

What makes this worse than a typical lost update is that nothing in the system is wrong afterwards. The truck row is internally consistent, both shipments say ASSIGNED, no constraint was violated and no error was logged. The contradiction only exists across two rows nobody compares, so it is discovered by a human at a loading dock where one truck has been promised to two shipments — hours later, with a driver and a customer both present.

The window looks small and is not: allocation involves a geo filter, a ranking pass and two round trips, so it is tens of milliseconds wide, and bookings for the same region cluster in time because demand is not uniform through the day.

  • Race condition: two Allocation Service instances both see the truck as available, both try to assign. One succeeds, other overwrites – or worse, both succeed with different shipments.

Use as an atomic CAS ().

Same as Good + retry with pre-sorted candidates.

3) The truck has not moved in three hours. Why does the ETA still say 40 minutes?

Problem: FR3 computes an ETA once, at booking, from a straight line and an assumed speed. Every input to it is wrong, and it is never revisited.

Bad: exactly FR3 — straight-line distance over average speed, computed once.

Two independent errors compound. The distance is wrong because roads are not straight: a route around a bay, through hills, or restricted to a permitted truck corridor can run 40% longer than the line between its endpoints. The speed is wrong because a single average ignores terrain, load weight, mandatory driver rest periods and traffic.

But the disqualifying property is that it is computed once. A truck delayed three hours still displays its original arrival time, so the ETA is least accurate at precisely the moment the shipper most needs it — and because nothing recomputes, no part of the system is aware the number is now fiction. A stale ETA is worse than no ETA, because the shipper plans a dock crew around it.

  • Ignores traffic, road network, stops, detours. Off by hours on long routes.

A stale ETA is worse than no ETA, because the shipper plans a dock crew around it.

Recompute every 2 minutes for active shipments + anomaly detection.

4) Every shipper polls every 5 seconds to hear the truck moved 40 metres. Who is that serving?

Problem: FR2 has the shipper’s app ask repeatedly whether anything changed. The answer is almost always trivial, and the asking is what costs.

Bad: the polling FR2 built — GET /shipments/{id}/location every 5 seconds per watching shipper. Each request is a full HTTP round trip plus a database read to return a position that moved a few tens of metres, and the request rate scales with how many people are watching rather than with how much is happening.

The latency argument is the one that settles it. A 5-second poll means the map is on average 2.5 seconds stale and at worst 5, before rendering — and tightening the interval to improve that multiplies the request rate by the same factor. There is no interval that is both fresh and affordable, which is the signature of using the wrong mechanism rather than the wrong number.

  • 5K active shippers x 1 req/5s = 1K req/sec. Most responses are identical to the previous (truck hasn’t moved much in 5s). Wasteful.

+ debounce + Redis Pub/Sub for routing.

13. Design Self-Audit

Potential weakness Assessment
Dedicated search index? Not needed – we’re not doing text search. Geo queries handled by Redis Geo.
Stale reads after writes? Allocation reads from Postgres (source of truth, not cache). Tracking reads from Redis with 10s staleness – acceptable.
Single point of failure (SPOF)? Redis: use Redis Cluster with replicas. Kafka: 3 brokers with replication factor 2. Postgres: primary + sync replica.
Dead-letter for async failures? Kafka consumer failures: retry 3x, then send to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) topic. Alert ops for manual review.
Data freshness across change data capture (CDC) and cache? Truck status in Postgres is the source of truth. Redis Geo is updated from Kafka (eventual, <1s lag). Allocation reads Postgres for assignment (strong).
Cost at hot tiers? Redis: 50K entries x 100 bytes = 5MB. Trivial. Kafka: 300K msg/sec x 100 bytes x 24h retention = ~2.5TB/day. Moderate. Use tiered storage.
scroll →

14. Core Flows

Booking Flow (end-to-end)

Tracking Flow (real-time)

Shipment State Machine

PENDING --> ASSIGNED --> PICKED_UP --> IN_TRANSIT --> DELIVERED
    |           |                          |
    v           v                          v
 CANCELLED   CANCELLED                 DELAYED --> IN_TRANSIT

15. Final Architecture

New components: four boxes here were earned in the deep dives rather than introduced by a functional requirement.

  • Kafka + Location Ingestion: the ingestion path from Deep Dive 1. Pings land in the log, a consumer applies them to Redis, so the 300K-per-second tier never touches Postgres.
  • Redis Geo + Cache: current truck positions and cached ETAs. This is the store allocation searches and tracking reads; Postgres remains the source of truth for who owns what.
  • WebSocket Service + Redis Pub/Sub: the push path from Deep Dive 4. Pub/Sub carries a position from the machine that received it to the machine holding the shipper’s open connection.
  • ETA Service: the recomputation loop from Deep Dive 3. It wakes up every two minutes for shipments in transit, asks the Maps API how long the remaining route now takes, and publishes the new number.
  • Cassandra (history): the append-only archive of truck paths, for replay, disputes and analytics - never on the allocation or tracking hot path.
